feedback: When the squeezed sponge springs back but the squeezed dough stays flat, point out the contrast directly: the same action gave different outcomes because they are made of different materials.
If a child predicts the dough will spring back, run the let-go test and let the observed result do the teaching rather than just telling them.
When a child tries to squash the wooden stick (or stone) and it barely moves, name the third case: some materials do not change shape this way when we use our hands.
Reinforce after every trial that the material is still the same — the squashed dough is still dough, the bent wire is still metal.
activities.intendedInsight: Materials respond differently to the same action: squeeze a sponge and it springs back, squeeze dough and it stays flattened, and squeeze a thick wooden stick or a stone and it barely changes. Likewise, a stretched elastic band snaps back while twisted soft wire stays twisted. So 'everything springs back' is not true, and the result can depend on the action as well as the material. Across all of this, the material itself is unchanged.
learnerActions: Choose a material from a varied set — playdough/plasticine, an elastic band, a sponge, a thick wooden stick or block, a stone, soft wire, paper.
Pick one of the four actions and apply it: press/squeeze to squash, curve it to bend, hold each end and turn opposite ways to twist, pull to stretch.
Watch the material deform as the force is applied (dough flattens, wire coils, elastic thins).
Release ('let go') and observe what happens: does it snap back to its old shape, stay in the new shape, or barely move?
Record the result for each material and the action you used in a comparison grid: springs back / stays changed / won't change this way.
Note each time that the material is still the same stuff — e.g. a tag or label 'this is still WOOD' — so the shape changed but the material did not.
activities.title: Materials deformation bench: apply a force, then let go

feedback: If a child only pushes/squashes regardless of the instruction, model each of the four actions once with a spare material — this is a procedural gap, so focus on the action, not on material properties.
Confirm the distinct hand movement for each: a twist needs two ends turned opposite ways, a stretch needs a pull.
activities.intendedInsight: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching are four distinct actions, not one generic 'push'. Being able to produce each one distinctly is needed before comparing how materials respond.
learnerActions: Learn each action with a precise, embodied definition: squash = press/squeeze; bend = curve so it is not straight; twist = hold each end and turn opposite ways; stretch = pull to change its shape.
Perform each action with your own hands first (turn your hands to twist, pull to stretch) before touching a material.
Match each action word to a demonstration or picture of that action.
Say the definition aloud (with audio support for pre/early readers).
activities.title: Embody and define the four actions

feedback: Where a prediction was wrong (e.g. you expected the clay to spring back), treat the surprise as the learning: the same action gave a different result because the material is different.
Use the completed table to compare two materials side by side — clay squashes and stays; a thick piece of wood barely bends.

If a child says a rigid material just 'wasn't pushed hard enough', agree that a much bigger force might bend or break it, but explain that with the force our hands can give it does not change shape this way — that is what we observed.
activities.intendedInsight: Predicting first surfaces your idea so the evidence can confirm or overturn it; recording in a table supports comparing and classifying materials by how they respond.
learnerActions: Before handling each material, predict how it will respond to a chosen action: will it spring back, stay changed, or barely change?
Test your prediction by hand and compare what happened to what you expected.

Sort the materials into three groups for the action you tested (a different action can give a different result): springs back (e.g. squeezed sponge, stretched elastic band), stays changed (e.g. squashed dough, bent soft wire), won't change this way by hand (e.g. squeezed thick wood, stone).
Build a simple table with the material down the side and columns for 'springs back?', 'stays changed?', 'won't change?'.
activities.title: Predict, then test, and sort by how materials respond

feedback: If a child says the squashed clay 'isn't clay any more', show it is the same clay, the same weight, and can be rolled back into a ball — only the shape changed.
Connect the weighing result to the idea: nothing was added or removed, so it is the same material with the same weight.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing an object's shape does not change the material it is made of and does not make new material — squashed clay is still clay, bent metal is still metal, and the weight stays the same because nothing was added or taken away.
learnerActions: Take a lump of clay, roll it into a ball, then squash it flat — look at the before and after.
Explain whether it is still clay after being squashed, and how you could show it is the same stuff (e.g. roll it back into a ball).
Weigh a ball of clay, squash it, and weigh it again; compare the two weights.
Do the same reasoning for a bent metal paperclip: is it still metal after bending?
activities.title: Same material, new shape: show the stuff is unchanged
